articles.title: Enabling FIPS on UAT Postgres servers meant moving off MD5 passwords
articles.excerpt: The problem We needed FIPS mode enabled on our UAT database servers, running RHEL 9.5. The reason was an RBI audit point, so it was not optional. The first attempt to enable FIPS did not stick, and th…
articles.body: The problem We needed FIPS mode enabled on our UAT database servers, running RHEL 9.5. The reason was an RBI audit point, so it was not optional. The first attempt to enable FIPS did not stick, and the reason was on the database side: our Postgres databases were still using the older MD5 password hashing method, which is not compatible with FIPS mode. Why this mattered more than a usual config change These are not isolated databases. Our UAT Keycloak identity provider runs on them, and the dependency chain goes like this: If Postgres is down, Keycloak does not run. If Keycloak is down, Superset does not run. If Vault is down, all the application pods end up stuck in CrashLoopBackOff.
articles.author: Afzal Hassan

articles.title: Logrotate for Application Logs: Configure Rotation Without Losing Data
articles.excerpt: Application logs can grow until they fill a VPS disk, but deleting a large log file by hand is not always a fix. A running process may keep writing to the file it already has open—even after you remov…
articles.body: Application logs can grow until they fill a VPS disk, but deleting a large log file by hand is not always a fix. A running process may keep writing to the file it already has open—even after you remove its directory entry. The safer approach is to configure log rotation and tell the application how to reopen its logs. This guide sets up logrotate for a custom application that writes to /var/log/myapp/app.log . The example assumes the application runs as the myapp user and can reopen its log when it receives SIGUSR1 . Check your application’s documentation before choosing a signal; not every program handles it the same way.

articles.title: AI Needs a Test That Fights Back
articles.excerpt: One right answer is not the same as a good sequence of decisions. eSlams is building a public stadium to explore the difference. Have you ever replayed a game in your head and traced the loss back to…
articles.body: One right answer is not the same as a good sequence of decisions. eSlams is building a public stadium to explore the difference. Have you ever replayed a game in your head and traced the loss back to a single move? Sometimes, one overlooked threat is enough to undo a game’s worth of good decisions. That is what makes an opponent different from an answer key. On a fixed question-and-answer test, the response is the end of the task. In a game, it is the beginning of the next problem. Your opponent responds. New information changes what makes sense. A promising plan becomes a liability. You have to adjust, carrying the consequences of your last decision into the next one. So what happens when an AI model has to do more than produce a convincing answer?

articles.title: Brakes Let You Go Fast: Balancing Acceleration and Safety for AI Agents
articles.excerpt: Written by John Feminella We now inhabit a world where agents can execute operations in production environments and at the speed of light. The question many are now grappling with: How can we ensure s…
articles.body: Written by John Feminella We now inhabit a world where agents can execute operations in production environments and at the speed of light. The question many are now grappling with: How can we ensure safety for agentic systems with access to powerful operations, without handcuffing what they can accomplish? The problem I think about this a lot in the context of the controls we’ve introduced at Two Sigma to limit risks from agents. At a regulated firm, too little safety is an existential risk, and too little innovation is a slow death. If we want to reap the benefits of agents, we must do so in a way that gives us both safety and freedom to innovate. As John Shedd wrote, “A ship in harbor is safe — but that is not what ships are for.” For us, we started with five essential ingredients.

articles.title: What 1,368 Real-World AI Incidents Teach Us About Evaluation
articles.excerpt: AI evaluation has become increasingly sophisticated at testing individual models. We measure accuracy, test hallucinations, run fairness checks, evaluate robustness, and compare systems against increa…
articles.body: AI evaluation has become increasingly sophisticated at testing individual models. We measure accuracy, test hallucinations, run fairness checks, evaluate robustness, and compare systems against increasingly demanding benchmarks. Yet when we studied real-world AI failures, one pattern kept appearing: many of the failures that mattered most were not really model failures alone. They emerged after the model entered a real operational environment. A model can perform well during testing and still create problems because the data is incomplete, the workflow is poorly designed, monitoring is weak, or nobody can realistically intervene once something goes wrong.

articles.body: Using the NASA X-ray spacecraft Swift combined with radio observations, astronomers have observed a supermassive black hole burping radio jets 300 days after a heavy cosmic meal. The team was also able to roughly estimate the mass of this feeding cosmic titan, which sits at the heart of the Perseus Cluster, a massive collection of thousands of galaxies. The black hole sits at the center of the galaxy NGC 1275, located around 225 light-years away, and is the brightest galaxy of the Perseus Cluster . The supermassive black hole first flared in X-rays, which indicated an increase in the rate at which it was accreting matter.

articles.title: The moon could turn astronauts into 'walking, high voltage capacitors' that accidentally zap spacecraft
articles.excerpt: NASA is asking for ideas to stop static electricity from zapping astronauts or critical hardware during moon missions.
articles.body: NASA is asking for ideas to stop static electricity from zapping astronauts or critical hardware during moon missions. The agency opened a "Lunar Grounding Challenge" to avoid situations where an astronaut on the moon could become "a walking, high voltage capacitor." Submissions for the $150,000 competition are due Jan. 15 and you can see the requirements here . NASA is hoping to put astronaut boots at the lunar south pole in 2028 during the Artemis 4 or 5 missions, on the first landing mission since NASA's Apollo 17 in 1972. But simulations suggest that both "tribocharging" (electric-charge transfer between two objects) and plasma charging (from ambient gas in the region) could build up electric charge on spacesuits.

articles.body: NASA experiments focused on human and plant health and drug-resistant organisms will travel to the International Space Station aboard SpaceX’s 35th Commercial Resupply Services mission for the agency from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, advancing research that benefits life on Earth and future exploration. This research supports astronaut health during long-duration missions through four investigations from the agency’s Biological and Physical Sciences division, including 3D models of the human brain, a crop disease study, a faster way to assess astronaut health, and an analysis of antibiotic-resistant bacteria aboard the space station.

articles.title: The 'Halloween Fireballs' are coming. Here's what to expect from the Taurids this year
articles.excerpt: The Southern and Northern Taurid meteor showers will produce occasional bright, slow-moving meteors worldwide during October and November, with moon-free peaks in 2026.
articles.body: They don't produce anything like the torrent of "shooting stars" associated with August's Perseids or December's Geminids, but the Taurid meteor showers have something else going for them — fireballs. The Taurids are famous for occasionally producing exceptionally bright, slow-moving meteors that can streak dramatically across the night sky from September to December. As a bonus, they're visible from both the Northern and Southern hemispheres. That's because they appear to emanate from the constellation Taurus, which sits close to the ecliptic, the apparent path the sun takes across the sky as Earth orbits around it. The Taurids are actually two closely related showers — the Southern Taurids and Northern Taurids — whose activity overlaps in late October and November.
articles.author: Jamie Carter

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 12, 1964: The Soviet Union launches Voskhod 1, the 1st multi-person cosmonaut crew, into space
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 12, 1964, the Soviet Union launched Voskhod 1, a 24-hour crewed mission that achieved several "firsts" for human spaceflight. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 12, 1964, the Soviet Union launched Voskhod 1, a 24-hour crewed mission that achieved several "firsts" for human spaceflight . This was the first time that a spacecraft carried more than one person into orbit, with three cosmonauts packed inside the spacecraft. Only two cosmonauts were originally supposed to fly on this mission, but Soviet politicians pressured the Russian space program to add one more. This left no room for spacesuits on board, so this also became the first spaceflight without spacesuits . Two of the crewmembers, an engineer and a doctor, became the first civilians to go to space. On Oct. 12, 1964, the Soviet Union launched the first multiperson mission, Voskhod 1, which launched three Russian cosmonauts into space.
articles.author: Hanneke Weitering

articles.title: Namibian salt flats look like an alien planet | Space photo of the day for Oct. 12, 2026
articles.excerpt: The Etosha Pan in northern Namibia, the largest salt flat in the country, looks otherworldly in this satellite photo.
articles.body: The Etosha Pan, Namibia's largest salt pan, seen from space. (Image credit: Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2026), processed by ESA) A neon blue pool swirls amongst what look like clouds, all surrounded by a bright red stretch of land. This might look like the surface of an alien planet , but it's actually a salt flat right here on Earth , seen from space. What is it? Etosha National Park in northern Namibia hosts the largest salt pan, or piece of land covered with salt and other minerals, in the country. This image of the Etosha Pan was captured on April 5 of this year by Europe's Copernicus Sentinel-2 mission, which consists of two identical satellites in the same orbit.
articles.author: Chelsea Gohd
